USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep existing tariffs in place, do not fire the December 15 List 4B consumer tariffs while the Phase One text is being drafted, and do not unilaterally roll anything back. Drive the Washington talks to a written, enforceable Phase One (ag purchases, limited IP/currency/financial-services language, a workable dispute mechanism) and treat cancellation or delay of Dec 15 as the bargain, not a gift. Leave Huawei entity-list and later-phase structural issues (subsidies, forced tech transfer, industrial policy) off this tranche so a skinny deal can close without repeating the May collapse.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is mildly elevated, not high or existential. US agriculture remains the exposed export sector: China’s retaliation and the Aug 5 buying halt slashed soybean sales (2018 sales to China down ~74%), pork/soy faced stacked duties, and farm-belt allies (e.g. Grassley) warned of permanently lost markets even as USDA aid tried to paper over losses. US goods exports to China were still only ~$8.9bn in Oct vs ~$39.8bn of imports; industrial production slipped to 101.4 and Michigan sentiment cratered to 89.8 in August before recovering to 95.5. The Fed had already cut (fed funds 2.38% to 1.83%; 10-year yield from 2.51% to 1.78%). That is real GDP/politics drag, but it is not a tariff cascade into recession: VIX fell back to 12.33 by Oct 30, the goods deficit narrowed, and the Oct 11 Phase One announcement delayed the mid-October 25%→30% hike. The threat is therefore about unfinished business and a fragile truce, not an existential hit to supply chains or ally cohesion.

Action should stay near zero because the US still has usable leverage and because another escalation would be self-harming. China is asking to kill Dec 15 (phones, laptops, toys — Christmas consumer goods) and to walk existing lists back toward the original $250bn; Lighthizer and Mnuchin have explicitly left Dec 15 undecided. Giving that chip away before a signed text, or conceding large purchase numbers without paper, repeats the May 5–10 pattern when Beijing was accused of renegotiating and List 3 went to 25%. Escalating tariffs now would also blow up the only path that relieves farm pressure ($40–50bn annual ag buys touted by Trump; China already signaled soy/pork exemptions in mid-September) and would tax US retailers just as markets have calmed. Negotiate the text, keep Dec 15 live until signature, and do not trade Huawei relief or a broad tariff rollback for an unsigned handshake.
key_factors: Phase One announced Oct 11 but still unsigned; 3–5 weeks of drafting and a possible APEC signing
Dec 15 List 4B (~$156bn consumer goods) remains live US leverage; China wants it cancelled plus some existing-tariff rollback
US farm sector is the main retaliatory target (soy/pork duties, lost China market, political pressure in swing states)
Macro costs are real but contained: Fed easing, Aug sentiment shock, soft IP; VIX and yields eased after the truce
May 2019 collapse is the binding precedent against unpapered concessions
Structural/tech issues (Huawei entity list, subsidies, forced TT) are deferred and should stay deferred for this tranche

sources_cited.excerpt: After Washington talks, Trump announces a "Phase One" deal in principle: China to buy roughly $40–50B of US agricultural products annually; IP and currency issues also cited. Planned mid-October tariff hike delayed.

Trump tweets that negotiations are going "too slowly" and that China is attempting to "renegotiate." Orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
List 4A takes effect at 15% (~$110–125B of Chinese imports). China's first tranche of the ~$75B retaliation also takes effect.
Chinese state media reports soybeans, pork, and some other farm goods will be excluded from additional retaliatory tariffs (goodwill signal ahead of talks).
After CNY breaks 7 per USD, US Treasury designates China a currency manipulator (first such designation since 1994).
Michigan consumer sentiment fell from 98.4 in July to 89.8 in August, then recovered to 95.5 in October.
US industrial production eased from 102.44 (June) to 101.43 (October).
US goods exports to China remained depressed at $8.85bn in October versus $39.8bn of imports from China.
VIX spiked to 24.59 on 2019-08-05 and had fallen to 12.33 by 2019-10-30 after the Phase One announcement.
Federal funds effective rate cut from 2.38% (June) to 1.83% (October).

Lighthizer said no decision has been made yet on whether to suspend another wave of tariffs scheduled to take effect on Dec. 15. Huawei relief is not part of any deal. Grassley: a final deal must address structural issues and include strong enforcement.

USTR (Oct 25): sides are close to finalising some sections; deputy talks continue. China expected to ask the US to drop Dec 15 tariffs on ~$156bn (phones, laptops, toys) and seek removal of the Sept 1 15% tranche. Mnuchin: no decision on Dec 15.
Mnuchin: will not sign unless it is on paper. Trump acknowledged the agreement could fall apart in the 3–5 week drafting window. May collapse cited as precedent. Huawei not in the deal.
China targeted soy, pork, corn; ASA said sales had been at a virtual standstill; 2018 US soybean sales to China dropped 74%; Grassley warned farmers risk permanently losing an export market.
